title: Correlated Subquery to Window Function
description: A correlated scalar subquery is recomputed per row via a spool; a window function (COUNT(*) OVER ...) computes each group's value in one pass. Why it matters: correlated subqueries are a very natural first instinct for "a value about this row's group" -- knowing the window-function alternative is one of the highest-value modern SQL skills.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
One of the most common real-world reporting needs is showing a value 'about the group this row belongs to' right next to each individual row — for example, listing every order and, next to each one, showing how many total orders that same customer has ever placed. The very first instinct most developers reach for, and a completely understandable one, is a **correlated subquery**: a little SELECT nested inside the main query that references a column from the outer row, like `(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Orders o2 WHERE o2.CustomerId = o.CustomerId)`. It reads almost like plain English — 'for this row, count the orders where the customer matches' — and it produces the correct answer. The word 'correlated' specifically means the inner subquery isn't independent; it depends on (is correlated with) a value from the row currently being processed by the outer query, which is exactly why it can compute a per-customer answer for each row.

The problem is *how* SQL Server has to evaluate that correlated subquery under the hood. Logically, it has to run the inner COUNT once for every single outer row — if you're listing 100 orders belonging to, say, 30 different customers, the naive interpretation is running that inner count 100 separate times, even though many of those 100 rows share the same customer and would get the identical count. SQL Server is smart enough to notice this redundancy and tries to help by introducing a **spool** — a temporary cache, stored in a **Worktable** in tempdb, that holds previously computed subquery results so it doesn't have to redo identical work for rows sharing the same customer. This spooling optimization genuinely helps compared to the worst case, but it isn't free either: populating and repeatedly reading from that Worktable is itself a real cost, showing up as a large logical-read count against a table that has nothing to do with your actual data — it's pure internal bookkeeping overhead from the query pattern itself. And critically, this overhead scales with how many distinct groups and rows you have; as the order table and customer base grow, the spool grows right along with them, and what felt fine on test data with a handful of customers can become a real bottleneck once there are thousands.

There's a fundamentally better tool for exactly this 'value about my group, shown on every row of the group' pattern: a **window function**. `COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerId)` asks for something logically identical to the correlated subquery — a per-customer count, attached to every row for that customer — but SQL Server can compute it in a completely different, far more efficient way. Instead of repeatedly re-running an inner query, the engine can group (or 'segment') the rows by `CustomerId` in a single pass, tally up a count for each segment as it goes, and then stamp that already-computed count onto every row belonging to that segment. No re-evaluation per outer row, no correlated lookup, and critically, no spool worktable needed at all — the whole computation happens in one streaming or hash-based pass over the data, doing the counting work exactly once per customer instead of once per row.

Why does this distinction matter so much in practice? Because the correlated-subquery instinct is extremely natural and extremely common — 'show me this row's group total,' 'show me this customer's average order size next to every one of their orders,' 'flag whether this is the customer's first order' — these are everyday reporting requirements, and a correlated subquery is often the very first way people learn to express them, because it maps directly onto how you'd describe the requirement in English. Window functions, by contrast, are a comparatively newer and less universally taught part of SQL, so plenty of experienced developers never fully make the mental switch, even though window functions are usually both faster *and* often more concise once you're used to reading them. Recognizing 'oh, this correlated subquery is really just asking for a per-group value' and reflexively reaching for `OVER (PARTITION BY ...)` instead is one of the single highest-value modern SQL skills to build, because the pattern it replaces — a correlated subquery riding along with every outer row — shows up constantly across real reporting and dashboard code, and every one of those places is a candidate for this exact rewrite.

What to look for in a plan that has this problem: a **Worktable** (spool) operator with a meaningfully large logical-read count sitting alongside reads on the actual base table, often feeding into what looks like a nested-loop-style repeated lookup structure — the telltale sign that a correlated subquery's result is being cached and repeatedly consulted rather than computed once. The fix is a direct, mechanical rewrite: replace the correlated subquery expression with an equivalent windowed aggregate (`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, and others all support the same `OVER (PARTITION BY ...)` treatment), and the spool, along with its associated I/O overhead, disappears from the plan entirely.

## Scenario
A screen lists orders and, next to each, how many orders that customer has placed. It does it with a **correlated scalar subquery** — `(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Orders o2 WHERE o2.CustomerId = o.CustomerId)`. It works, but it does a lot of redundant counting.

## Why it's slow
The subquery is logically evaluated **once per outer row**, recomputing each customer's count over and over. SQL Server softens the blow by caching partial results in a **Worktable (spool)** in tempdb — but that spool is itself thousands of extra logical reads, and the pattern scales badly as rows and customers grow.

## What to look for
- A **Worktable** with a large logical-read count alongside the base table.
- A plan with a spool feeding a nested-loops-style repeated aggregate.

## The concept
Compute the per-group value **once** with a window function: `COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerId)`. SQL Server segments the rows by customer and counts each group in a single pass — no correlated re-evaluation, no spool worktable. Window functions (`OVER`) are the go-to replacement for "a value about this row's group" that people reach for correlated subqueries to express.
startingQuery:
SELECT TOP (100) o.OrderId, o.CustomerId,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Orders o2 WHERE o2.CustomerId = o.CustomerId) AS CustomerOrders
FROM Orders o
ORDER BY o.OrderId;
hints: The correlated subquery is evaluated per row; the plan caches it in a Worktable (spool) that costs thousands of reads.
You want each customer's count computed once, not once per order. A window function does exactly that.
Replace the subquery with COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY o.CustomerId).
